paragraphs.source_en: The dating of the Round Head paintings is also subjected to the high and low chronology. The supporters of the high chronology believe that the Round Heads are the oldest Central Saharan rock paintings made by hunter-gatherers in the Early Holocene. The scholars are still not agreed on the exact period of the origin, i. e. if it was in the Epipalaeolithic or Mesolithic period but the pre-Pastoral age is generally accepted. This would have started shortly after 10,000 BP, to when the archaeological remains related to the human occupation are attested, and it would have ended shortly before the appearance of domestic stock in the Central Sahara at 7,500 BP (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1996a).

paragraphs.source_en: The most controversial point among the supporters of the two different chronologies is whether Round Head art contained images of domesticated cattle or not. Jelinek (2004) states that at Afarh shelter in the Acacus a composition of the presumed Round Head style represents a possible taurokathapsia scene of human figures jumping over a bull, and he does not exclude other domesticated cattle images in the Round Head complex. He nevertheless places the origins of the Round Head art as early as the 10th millennium BP, proposing that the presumed domesticated cattle would belong to later phases. This opinion is shared by Soleilhavoup (2007) who claims that domesticated cattle are attested in the Round Head paintings but he acknowledges that this artistic tradition may have started before the Pastoral period.

paragraphs.source_en: The main supporter of the low chronology, Muzzolini, believes that the Round Heads were created by Neolithic groups with domesticated cattle, and they belong therefore to the Pastoral period. The earliest Central Saharan paintings would therefore be the Round Head and Pastoral styles, both placed after 7,000 BP when domestication is archaeologically confirmed in the Central Sahara (Muzzolini 1992; 1995a, b; 2003). However, the paintings that are claimed to be of the Round Head style and to represent domesticated cattle are often very controversial, in that neither the style nor the domestication are certain.
